abstract: Centrosomes comprise a pair of centrioles that organise a surrounding pericentriolar material (PCM) that usually grows as cells prepare to enter mitosis, stops growing during mitosis, and then shrinks as cells exit mitosis. In most models of centrosome growth, the PCM stops growing because cells run out of a limiting component. Using experiments and mathematical modelling in the early Drosophila embryo, we show that the embryonic cell cycle oscillator (CCO) can generate these centrosome growth kinetics without relying on the depletion of a limiting component. At the start of each cycle centrioles assemble two dynamic and interconnected PCM scaffolds comprising Spd-2/CEP192 and Cnn/CDK5RAP2. As embryos approach mitosis, rising CCO activity destabilises the Spd-2 scaffold, slowing centrosome growth, but stabilises the Cnn scaffold, locking it into a low-dynamic state. At the end of mitosis CCO activity drops, triggering rapid Cnn scaffold disassembly. Thus, the CCO drives centrosome growth dynamics by regulating the stability of two interconnected PCM scaffolds.
